item.title: U.S. and Iran officials meet in New York to discuss ending the war
item.description:
President Trump said U.S. officials met for three hours with the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

  • "It was a good meeting ... It's to their advantage to make a deal," Trump said before meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
  • A U.S. official and a regional source said Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attended the meeting from the U.S. side, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi from the Iran side.
  • Iran state television said the meeting was requested by the U.S. and "driven by the need to convey Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz," which include lifting the naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending the war on all fronts.

Why it matters: The General Assembly offers a rare opportunity to try to break the stalemate in the war, which is approaching the seven-month mark with no signs of a breakthrough.

  • It's the first meeting between U.S. and Iranian officials since mid-June.

State of play: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC Tuesday morning that President Trump is open to meeting with the Iranians in New York "because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems." He added, however, that no meeting has been scheduled yet.

  • Trump is expected to meet with representatives of nine Arab countries on Tuesday to discuss the war. Many of the countries are expected to urge Trump to de-escalate with Iran and work to reach a deal, regional sources said.

What he said: In his speech before the UN General Assembly, Trump reiterated what he told Axios last week: that he has "a big decision to make" whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilating the Islamic Republic."

  • Trump said he thinks the U.S. will reach a deal with Iran after the midterms
  • "We will get it done one way or another. We will get it done and get it done fast," Trump said.
  • "It doesn't make sense for Iran not to (make a deal)," he added. "They are waiting to see how I do in the midterm elections. What they don't realize is that I am not running … I will be here for two-and-a-half years. I gave no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."

Zoom out: Trump also made a broader case for the war, saying many presidents before him ignored the Iran threat for many years.

  • "After giving Iran every chance for a deal I took action to ensure that neither the U.S. nor any other nation will have to face such a catastrophic problem," Trump said.

Zoom in: Trump said Iran violated the ceasefire by attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Still, he added, the U.S. manages to get dozens of oil tankers out of the strait every night.

  • "We must be united in putting pressure on Iran. I call on all countries to join us in our pressure campaign against Iran," he said.

This story has been updated with new details.

item.title: Trump backs ban on diesel exports
item.description:
President Trump said during a Tuesday press interview alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that he has also called for a ban on U.S. diesel exports, joining other conservative voices who back the policy.

Why it matters: Trump's endorsement marks a shift for an administration that has resisted calls to restrict fuel exports, as record diesel prices squeeze farmers and truckers and fuel Republican concerns ahead of the midterms.

  • Economists and energy analysts the move could lower diesel prices for Americans in the short term but would likely raise prices globally including eventually in the U.S.

Thought bubble, via Axios' Ben Geman: The politics of $6.50 diesel are quickly overwhelming a broad consensus among oil market analysts that an export ban could ultimately backfire.

What they're saying: When asked if he supported a diesel ban endorsed by other Republicans, he said, "I've called for that too."

  • "I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel, and it could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know it's a sort of a flow, it's a balance. But no, I've called for it. I've called for it within my people."

Catch up quick: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) recently proposed blocking diesel exports, hoping to lower prices domestically, and other farm-state Republicans quickly signed on too.

  • Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who faces a competitive re-election race, called for a diesel ban Monday while slamming the war in Iran.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said last week that he was "open" to an export ban.

Zoom in: A ban would keep diesel that otherwise would be exported in the U.S., potentially increasing domestic supplies and lowering prices in the short term.

  • But analysts warn it could drive up global diesel prices and eventually feed higher costs back into the U.S. economy.
  • The U.S. has rarely resorted to outright energy export bans because of concerns about disrupting global markets.

Flashback: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said last week the administration would consider an export ban if it would lower prices, "but that's not the case."

Zoom out: Trump does have emergency powers that could allow him to enforce a ban.

  • Congress could also pass legislation to achieve the same goal, but Senate Republicans are significantly divided on the measure.
  • Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) questioned whether a ban was worth rocking global markets, calling it a "short-term" benefit … "that doesn't really move the needle."
  • Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) called it "a gimmick."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Cheap, powerful AI models are increasing usage, a bullish sign for the AI boom
item.description:
AI companies have competed on having the best and often most dangerous models for years. Now, they're pivoting to a new focus: cost.

Why it matters: The biggest risk to the AI boom is demand, and recent innovations to make models cheaper while maintaining powerful levels of intelligence have offered a bullish signal.

  • As the prices of top models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others come down, usage is increasing dramatically, a trend that points to the kind of demand that will be necessary to justify trillions of dollars in spending.

State of play: It's modelpalooza in the AI world this week, with OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and some Chinese model providers all offering new releases. Most of them are offering shocking levels of intelligence at prices that would've been unthinkable just a few months ago.

  • OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Tuesday, which brings down the cost for top business customers by 50% from previous iterations of the same models, the company shared with Axios.
  • Anthropic is releasing Opus 5.5 on Tuesday, which the company says costs around 40% less to run than Opus 5 while maintaining top intelligence.
  • Elon Musk's xAI on Monday released Grok 4.7, pitching the new model around price-performance. Yet in a testament to the sheer brutality of competition in the AI race, it only took 24 hours for new options to wipe out much of that price advantage.

Threat level: The ferocity and speed of the race during an ongoing price war is an issue for OpenAI and Anthropic, which need to retain customers and revenue growth to justify their sky-high multi-trillion-dollar valuations.

Yes, but: Even as they face margin pressure, the trend is positive for the AI boom overall, as the price reductions make it much easier to bet on a bright future for AI use.

Follow the money: There is emerging evidence that cost cutting is a rising tide that can lift revenues for all AI providers.

  • In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token costs are fueling additional usage, and overall AI spending is increasing. That points to higher eventual profits for labs or any company providing the computing firepower that services AI usage.
  • Morgan Stanley sees competition from Chinese providers as yet another bullish signal for AI because it will just increase overall demand for computing by capturing more customers who can now access AI for less.
  • This concept is referred to in classic economic theory as Jevons Paradox, which holds that when technology brings down the cost of a resource, consumption increases.

Between the lines: Open-weight model companies, primarily coming out of China, have been on a tear in recent weeks.

  • DeepSeek this month released V4.1 Flash, which it says beats its previous flagship offering on a number of benchmarks with technical updates that allow the company to charge less for its intelligence.
  • That model is now number one on OpenRouter's leaderboard with a 172% spike in usage this week.

Reality check: Lowering costs to take market share isn't new in the AI world.

  • AI companies have a long history of releasing a new model and then lowering the cost for prior releases, or even releasing "flash" versions of larger models that are smaller and cheaper to run.
  • But the increased competition from open-weight model providers and their massive rise in leaderboards is fueling a broader focus on cost across offerings from top AI labs.

The bottom line: AI sticker shock feels like a distant memory given the massive push from labs to deliver cheaper models.

item.title: Exclusive: Trump adviser ties high gas prices to refining
item.description:
The affordability of gasoline remains "the top issue that the president looks at," Trump energy adviser Jarrod Agen said at an Axios House event Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Trump administration is championing energy savings from its deregulatory push as overseas conflicts, including the Iran war, rattle oil markets, driving up fuel costs and threatening an expensive winter for millions of households.

  • Tuesday's national average gas price was roughly $4.48, up from around $3.18 a year ago, per AAA.

Driving the news: Asked by Axios' Amy Harder if the president takes responsibility for the higher prices Americans are paying, Agen said that the president's "long-term goal is preventing Iran" from having "nuclear capabilities."

  • "He says the long term is worth it to stop them from having a nuclear weapon."

Flashback: Asked last year what a successful term would look like once the administration's time in Washington is up, Agen told Axios' Mike Allen that the one factor the president always looks at is the price at the pump.

  • "We want to make sure that U.S. consumers are paying not high prices on their electricity bills and gas," he said. "That is the key that ... drives us every single day."

Zoom in: Pressed on those remarks, Agen told Harder it's "still the top issue the president looks at" and attributed the price pain to strained refining capacity.

  • "We've got crude flowing," he said, though the full picture of how much oil is leaving the Strait of Hormuz isn't yet entirely clear.
  • "More crude is on the market, and so that's great. But refining capacity is the issue we're trying to solve, both domestically and then globally," Agen said. "If you look at refining capacity, Russia, for example, it's down 30, 40% China is not at their capacity."
  • He floated the possibility of relief via the Defense Production Act, which Trump already invoked, and infrastructure projects "to attack the refining issue."

Catch up quick: The national average diesel price shattered its record earlier this month and then topped $6 a gallon for the first time, threatening higher inflation and household costs amid already elevated fuel prices.

  • An estimate from Brown University found that the war in Iran has cost U.S. consumers more than $100 billion in higher energy prices, adding to the administration's affordability challenges ahead of the midterms as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.
  • Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and other compounding crises have put American refineries operating near maximum capacity to an unprecedented test and raised questions about whether the administration would place an export ban on American diesel.

What he's saying: Trump addressed the General Assembly gathering Tuesday, teling fellow world leaders that he "gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran."

Go deeper: Gas prices are rising again — and so is GOP grief in the midterms

item.title: Love is pricey. Here's what young Americans are doing about it
item.description:
Data: Zelle New Economics of Dating Report; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Rising costs are changing dating for more than eight in 10 Gen Z and millennial daters, leaving some to stop courting altogether, per new data from Zelle.

The big picture: Young Americans are pushing off milestones under cost pressures — and the milestones themselves, from getting hitched to buying a home, are getting pricier once they get there.

Driving the news: For younger Americans, just planning a date is a costly ordeal, with 17% of active Gen Z and Millennial daters saying they've gone into debt trying to maintain the dating lifestyle.

  • Nearly one-third say they've gone on fewer dates amid rising costs. A smaller share, 11%, say they've stopped dating because they couldn't afford it.
  • Members of Gen Z are more likely to split the cost of a date because of rising costs (26%) than Millennials (18%).
  • Daters have changed strategies to lighten the cost burden — like suggesting free activities and spending more time on dates at home, which were used by 37% and 33% of active daters, respectively.

The intrigue: As costs weigh on younger Americans, perhaps it's unsurprising that checkbook chemistry plays a big role in their love stories: Half of active daters say financial compatibility has at some point mattered more than romantic chemistry when deciding to keep dating someone.

  • Men are more likely to say that than women (56% versus 45%), as are Gen Zers (53%) than Millennials (46%).
  • But be warned: Talking money too much can kill the mood. For example, complaining about the price of everything or chatting too much about income would both give 47% of daters the "ick."

What they're saying: "Dating has always come with unspoken rules, but rising costs are forcing a rewrite," Denise Leonhard, general manager of Zelle, said in a statement.

  •  "Financial compatibility is becoming part of the chemistry test. The new flex isn't running up the tab; it's reading the room, respecting the budget and showing thought."

Zoom out: It comes as nearly all younger Americans (96%) reported being concerned about the cost of rent, groceries, gas or utilities, according to a recent Axios-Generation Lab poll of 18- to 34-year-olds.

  • With the Game of Life ahead of them, high costs are leaving younger Americans struggling to even get on the board.

Methodology: This online survey of 1,800 U.S. adults ages 18 and older was fielded August 14–25. Statistical testing is reported at the 95% confidence level.

Go deeper: Youth poll: Thumbs down on everything

item.title: A GOP senator wants Trump Jr. subpoenaed after Russian oligarch-funded wedding
item.description:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) is urging Senate Judiciary leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to investigate whether presidential family ties have been used for private family gain.

Why it matters: The Republican Curtis is pressing a Republican-led Senate committee to scrutinize President Trump's eldest son, arguing the same congressional oversight applied to Hunter Biden should apply to presidential families of both parties.

Driving the news: The Monday letter to Senate Judiciary chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) asks for an investigation into "private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access" tied to presidential family relationships.

  • Curtis wants the committee to subpoena both sons to testify about "any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value."

Catch up quick: ProPublica reported that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.'s three-day wedding celebration in the Bahamas, including buying a private-island rental.

  • Curtis also cited Trump Jr.'s ties to prediction markets. Trump Jr. is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket's advisory board. 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. is a partner, has invested in Polymarket.
  • Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments.

What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now."

For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment.

  • Hunter Biden has denied involving his father in business dealings.
  • Trump Jr. confirmed Kremlev hosted celebrations, describing it as a wedding gift from a friend. President Trump later defended the arrangement as "totally allowed" and said he had been told his son would repay Kremlev.

Flashback: House Republicans subpoenaed Hunter Biden in 2023 as part of their impeachment inquiry into then-President Biden.

  • The younger Biden testified that he did not involve his father in his business dealings.

  • Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments.

What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now."

For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment.

  • Hunter Biden has denied involving his father in business dealings.
  • Trump Jr. confirmed Kremlev hosted celebrations, describing it as a wedding gift from a friend. President Trump later defended the arrangement as "totally allowed" and said he had been told his son would repay Kremlev.

Flashback: House Republicans subpoenaed Hunter Biden in 2023 as part of their impeachment inquiry into then-President Biden.

  • The younger Biden testified that he did not involve his father in his business dealings.

item.title: The AI doomsday fear hidden in self-improving AI
item.description:
Of the various ways experts fear AI could kill us all, one is slowly moving closer to reality: AI learning to make itself unstoppable.

Why it matters: Recursive Self Improvement, the ability of an AI model to build better versions of itself without human guidance, could make increasingly capable systems harder for humans to control.

  • The RSI threshold doesn't represent danger by itself, but a lack of human control combined with rogue AI agents is a scenario that safety-conscious AI researchers have long feared.

Driving the news: Researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI say the process of training new models has grown more automated, coming close to the RSI rubicon.

  • An OpenAI employee told The Information the company has largely automated training new experimental models, with AI systems running experiments as directed by humans and correcting much of their work.
  • Last week, Anthropic shared that its AI training is becoming more automated, with AI leading about 26% of Anthropic's R&D work. AI collaborates on 90% of work, the company says.
  • "AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves," the company said.

Reality check: Critics say the milestone is more a function of coding automation than a marker of impending doom or inevitable AI superpowers.

  • While there's been an uptick in troubling AI security incidents in which models outstripped human control, some industry figures see those episodes as evidence of poor internal controls by OpenAI and other companies.
  • Further evidence of that view emerged this week, when The Wall Street Journal reported that independent security researchers used Anthropic's Claude to break into OpenAI in July.

Where does RSI come from?

Flashback: The concept behind RSI emerged in the 1950s as artificial intelligence became an area of study.

  • British mathematician and statistician Irving John Good described the idea in a 1965 paper: "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control."

How RSI could lead to AI doom

Threat level: Anthropic has warned RSI "might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems."

  • Some researchers theorize that advanced AI could resist shutdown or modification if staying operational helped it accomplish its goals.
  • Researchers into the hack by OpenAI agents into Hugging Face said the agents showed signs of this behavior.

Another concern: Self-improving AI systems capable of copying themselves could create a kind of digital natural selection, favoring systems that are best at acquiring compute, money and power to grow fastest.

  • In a darker version of this scenario, AI would be competing with humans for resources and power, experts say.

Between the lines: Dangerous behavior might not stop with one generation of AI.

  • Anthropic researchers found that some unwanted traits could pass from one model to another through training data, raising concerns that problematic behavior could persist across generations of AI.

How close are we to RSI?

The big picture: We're not there yet. A new analysis published this week found that AI feedback loops aren't yet hitting the RSI benchmarks.

What we're watching: Attempts at building RSI.

  • China's z.AI says they're heading toward RSI, where the models are helping build better infrastructure for better models.
  • Google DeepMind researchers published a framework for "Dream-RSI," a system that recursively improves how an AI agent finds solutions.

The bottom line: RSI isn't here yet, but it's a looming issue that's got the AI world on watch.

Go deeper: AI's architects say the next era of human history is here

item.title: With $7 trillion on the line, AI safety may always take a backseat to market domination
item.description:
The race for AI supremacy between labs, companies and countries may be impossible to reconcile with the push for AI safety, industry insiders tell Axios.

Why it matters: The top AI companies are proposing more independent oversight as they seek to engineer an AI slowdown. But trillions of dollars in incentives to keep pushing the frontier — and the money required for such scaling — will always loom larger, critics say.

State of play: As AI CEOs pitch the public on self-policing mechanisms and the use of third-party evaluators to make sure their models behave, those same models are sharing less about how they respond to questions and come up with solutions to problems.

  • The sheer complexity of AI systems, as well as the deployment of thousands of somewhat autonomous agents for a variety of tasks, will make real-time auditing or reviewing extremely difficult.
  • There is a trust gap for independent safety groups due to concerns about close ties between the industry and some evaluators, as well as a shared pool of investors and funders in the AI research community.

Follow the money: The incentive for speed is a lot more lucrative than the push to slow down in favor of safety.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to go public at multi-trillion-dollar valuations, and the companies face pressure to offer incrementally better and better models to justify those valuations.
  • More than $7 trillion will be spent scaling AI over the next five years, per Goldman Sachs. Frontier labs will have to generate a profit on that investment, which means outpacing competitors.
  • That includes keeping customers from pivoting to open-weight model providers, which can be cheaper to run and are viewed by some as a safer alternative.

Between the lines: AI is getting harder for anyone to monitor, making it unclear how the seemingly conflicted priorities of safety and rapid-fire model improvement can coexist.

  • Daniel Kokotajlo, former OpenAI researcher and executive director of the AI Futures Project, said he doesn't believe AI can be safely scaled.
  • Top AI companies should avoid putting the vast computing firepower at their disposal toward model improvement, a step that would force a slowdown, said Kokotajlo, whose team published the famed AI 2027 and 2040 essays.
  • Researchers and AI employees involved in scaling "are doing something wrong," he said.

Zoom in: Kokotajlo left OpenAI because of his own safety concerns in 2024.

  • Since then, he's been invited to give talks to current employees about his research on AI safety.
  • "The companies are just having this continuous process of conflicted feelings and internal discussion about like, what are we doing," he said. "Should we stop? Are we the good guys?"

Reality check: Plenty of others, including President Trump, see a safe future for AI and point to the potential for liability — civil or criminal — if companies fail to make their products safe.

  • "Whoever wins AI, WINS!" Trump wrote on Truth Social, reiterating that he won't be stifling or slowing down AI.
  • "Human willpower is capable of figuring out how to safely scale these models," Akshay Krishnaswamy, chief architect at Palantir, told Axios, adding that one way to achieve this is through open models.

The bottom line: As the industry is swept up in a riptide of AI slowdown rhetoric, it's unclear whether that's achievable in the near term.

item.title: U.S.-China "red telephone" could bring a Cold War guardrail to AI
item.description:
A distinctly Cold War calculus is looming over this week's Trump-Xi summit in Washington, as the U.S. and China weigh an emergency "red phone" for the day AI goes haywire.

Why it matters: U.S.-China relations are so brittle that an AI hotline — not a trade pact, strategic slowdown or diplomatic reset — could emerge as the summit's most meaningful outcome.

State of play: President Trump has spent the past week lashing out at AI "doomers" and boiling the race down to a single imperative: beat China.

  • Trump has called AI-catastrophe fears a "HOAX" and vowed the U.S. would "not in any way hinder or stifle" AI as it fights to preserve its lead over Beijing.
  • America's leading AI labs largely share Trump's urgency about China, but not his conclusion: many argue the intensity of the race is precisely why global safeguards are needed.

The other side: China is every bit as determined to win the AI race, but its leader Xi Jinping — who lands in Washington Wednesday for his first state visit since 2015 — is balancing two competing fears:

  1. Falling behind: Xi has no interest in a safety regime that freezes the race with America still ahead. Beijing is pushing cheap, capable open-source models around the world while portraying U.S. chip controls and calls for restraint as a calculated effort to keep China down.
  2. Losing control: Xi wants AI powerful enough to transform China's economy, but never so powerful that it slips beyond the control of the Communist Party. Beijing focuses less on Silicon Valley-style extinction scenarios than on nearer-term dangers, like cyberattacks, malicious use and disruptions to critical infrastructure.

Zoom in: That narrow overlap is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pitched Chinese officials this weekend on a "notification mechanism" for AI incidents with national-security implications.

  • The Cold War precedent is the hotline Washington and Moscow established after the Cuban Missile Crisis — a direct channel designed to keep accidents and ambiguity from escalating into nuclear Armageddon.
  • Trump and Xi are expected to discuss shared AI risks when they meet Thursday, while officials are also exploring a formal U.S.-China AI dialogue that could give the crisis channel a more permanent home.

Reality check: So far, nobody has publicly defined what would make the red phone ring.

  • In an AI catastrophe — say, a frontier model launches a major cyberattack on critical infrastructure — the first alarm may sound inside a private company rather than a military command center.
  • That gets thorny fast: The lab may know more than the government about what its model is doing, while officials would have to decide how much sensitive information to share before they fully understand the threat themselves.

Between the lines: Washington and Beijing already have crisis hotlines, as well as a history of going dark when they're needed most.

  • China suspended military contacts after Nancy Pelosi's 2022 Taiwan visit. Months later, Beijing declined a Pentagon request for a call after the U.S. shot down its surveillance balloon — precisely the kind of tense, ambiguous moments the channels were built to defuse.
  • COVID offered another warning: A cross-border threat that demanded transparency and cooperation instead fueled a bitter U.S.-China blame game over origins, information-sharing and responsibility.

The bottom line: The very existence of the proposal is an acknowledgment that AI is no longer just another arena of U.S.-China competition. A serious failure on either side could quickly become a shared crisis.

item.title: GOP's war for eyeballs
item.description:
Republicans are starting to trounce Democrats in political spending across the Senate map, and that advantage is now showing up in one of the metrics campaigns care about most: impressions.

Why it matters: Money matters in a campaign's closing weeks, but what campaigns are ultimately buying is voters' attention — and the price varies, depending on who is buying and when they place their ads.

  • Beginning in September, campaigns and super PACs start competing for the same finite supply of advertising inventory. But the campaigns are guaranteed lower rates.
  • Republicans are generating substantially more impressions — an estimate of the number of times an ad is seen — but their advantage isn't nearly as large as the spending disparity would suggest.

The intrigue: North Carolina is the only key battleground where Republicans have been spending more for fewer impressions in the first weeks of September.

  • Democrats generated 245 million impressions supporting former Gov. Roy Cooper, compared with 226 million for Republican Michael Whatley— even while being outspent by Republicans $10.6 million to $9 million.
  • Whatley has been consistently trailing Cooper in the polls.
  • It is forcing Republicans to weigh whether to begin pulling resources there. One key GOP super PAC took down $6.5 million worth of ads for October, as Semafor first reported.

By the numbers: From Sept. 1 through Sept. 17, Republican advertisers generated 502 million impressions in Texas, compared with 331 million for Democrats, according to data compiled by Kinetiq Political Insights.

  • Republicans, relying heavily on super PACs to bolster Attorney General Ken Paxton, spent $37 million over that period.
  • Democrats spent $9.5 million, with much of that coming directly from state Rep. James Talarico's campaign.

In Ohio: Republican ads generated 406 million impressions supporting Sen. Jon Husted, compared with 320 million for former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

  • Outside GOP groups accounted for much of Husted's advertising, with Republicans spending roughly $22 million on his behalf. Democrats spent $14 million for Brown.
  • Husted will get another boost. Fairshake, the crypto industry's main super PAC, has reserved $30 million in Ohio to oppose Brown.

Driving the news: Republicans opened up a massive spending advantage in September, outspending Democrats on air in nearly every competitive Senate race.

  • Those gaps have widened as more GOP-aligned super PACs have entered the fray.

Zoom out: Candidates get lower rates from broadcasters, meaning they get more airtime for fewer hard dollars than outside groups and super PACs.

  • Super PACs can raise unlimited sums, but often pay many times more than candidates for comparable broadcast inventory.

Zoom in: Democrats' strength in online fundraising has helped their candidates amass large hard-dollar war chests, while Republicans have countered with a significant advantage in super PAC and party money.

  • This year, a Supreme Court ruling opened the door for party committees to combine their funds with campaigns and get the lower rates.
  • The NRSC estimates that coordinated spending can make its advertising dollars stretch three to 10 times further than they did last cycle, Axios reported. It's committing $46.5 million to coordinated campaigns across eight states.

The bottom line: Republicans are relieved that the big-spending super PACs have arrived in force.

  • But that relief is tempered by concern that the cash infusion has come after some voters' views of the races and candidates may have already hardened.

item.title: Trump and Mamdani's unlikely rapport endures in New York
item.description:
President Trump and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani struck a warm tone Monday during their third in-person meeting and agreed to deepen talks over a major housing project in Queens.

Why it matters: The friendly encounter showed Trump and Mamdani's unusual personal rapport has endured despite their recent political clashes — and fresh disagreements on display Monday.

Driving the news: During their meeting, Trump and Mamdani agreed to step up talks over the mayor's plan to build 12,000 affordable homes on a deck over the sprawling Sunnyside Yard in Queens, the two said during a briefing after the talks.

  • "They've been talking about developing that for 50 years. So maybe they have a shot at doing it," said Trump, who met with Mamdani ahead of the UN General Assembly.

Zoom in: Their differences were also on display: Mamdani said all members of the press should be allowed White House access, moments before Trump defended his decision to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

  • Mamdani said he discussed his "very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorkers safe" with Trump during the meeting.
  • Still, Trump said he wanted Mamdani "to be a great mayor" and that he "certainly" has "great potential."

Context: Trump and Mamdani's first two White House meetings were unexpectedly cordial, and the two have kept in touch by text, Axios has reported.

Zoom out: Their policy differences have persisted, with tensions resurfacing recently over immigration and taxes.

  • New York City led a coalition of cities and counties in a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's new "public charge" immigration rule.
  • Trump has attacked the mayor's tax on luxury properties owned by nonresidents.

item.title: "People are pissed off": House Dems sneer as one of their own backs a Republican
item.description:
Rep. Jared Golden's decision to endorse one of House Republicans' most vulnerable incumbents is going down like a lead balloon among his fellow House Democrats.

Why it matters: The anger won't have much impact on Golden (D-Maine), who is retiring, but it could blow back on his closest ally, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.).

  • "People are pissed off," a House Democrat speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of private discussions told Axios, adding, "He is doing Gluesenkamp Perez no favors ... this will hurt her."
  • The Washington Democrat, who often breaks from party leadership and moves as a unit with Golden, "is going to have to figure out how she navigates around the suspicion this will create for her next Congress," this lawmaker said.
  • "He is leaving," said a senior House Democrat. "Marie is a bigger problem."

The other side: "I'm back home, grinding to bring back the gavels," Gluesenkamp Perez said in a statement to Axios.

  • "I really don't have energy to worry about the hurt feelings of anonymous colleagues."

Driving the news: Golden wrote an op-ed in a local newspaper in Rep. Mike Lawler's New York district endorsing the Republican for reelection.

  • Golden cited his work with Lawler on several pieces of legislation, most notably their bill to exempt lobstermen from certain federal environmental regulations.
  • "Mike Lawler has been a true partner to me and a friend to fishing families he will never represent," Golden wrote. "I strongly back him, and I hope voters send him back to work."

Between the lines: The endorsement comes after Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, who previously co-chaired the centrist Blue Dog Coalition, repeatedly broke with party leadership on key procedural votes in recent weeks.

  • Twice this month, the two Democrats provided Republican leadership with the votes needed to advance their legislation to the floor, including bills strongly opposed by Democratic leaders.
  • The repeated defections have sparked enormous anger within the House Democratic caucus, with some lawmakers calling to punish Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez.

What they're saying: Democrats met Golden's endorsement with contemptuous dismissal, arguing that it will do little to move the needle for a Republican in a district that went for former Vice President Harris in 2024.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a statement that Lawler is "peddling an 11th hour endorsement from a retiring Congressmember who represents an out of town district more than 400 miles away."
  • "That endorsement should get Mike an additional three votes — comprising most of the New Yorkers who have ever heard of Jared Golden," Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.) told Axios.
  • A third House Democrat who spoke on the condition of anonymity said similarly: "I don't think it's going to help Lawler. The people in that district who know who Golden is already know who they are voting for."

The intrigue: Just hours after the endorsement, House Democrats' main super PAC announced plans to spend millions more in the media market that encompasses Lawler's district.

  • House Majority PAC said it is reserving $2.45 million more on cable reservations in the New York City media market.
  • Some Democrats have argued against spending large sums to unseat Lawler, arguing that he is one of Republicans' most bipartisan and most politically formidable members.
  • Republicans have been massively outspending Democrats in Lawler's district.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from Gluesenkamp Perez.
item.content:encoded:

Why it matters: The anger won't have much impact on Golden (D-Maine), who is retiring, but it could blow back on his closest ally, Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.).

item.title: Ariz. activists build map to show federal agents at polls
item.description:
Arizona immigration advocates are building an interactive map to alert people if federal agents are spotted near polling places this fall.

Why it matters: It's illegal for federal law enforcement officers to interfere with the right to vote, but for months Republicans in D.C. and in Arizona's state house have floated the idea of ICE agents or National Guard troops being deployed to voting precincts.

  • When asked in May whether he was considering sending ICE or Guard troops to polling places, President Trump said he'd "do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections."
  • That raised concerns across the country about potential voter intimidation — particularly in places such as Arizona that have large immigrant populations.

The big picture: The online heat map of ICE activity that's being developed in Arizona will show live updates of polling places where ICE agents are spotted, along with past enforcement activity in Maricopa and Pima counties, the state's two most populous counties.

  • There's been a noticeable increase in ICE activity in these counties recently, said Karime Rodriguez, a spokesperson for the Arizona Center for Empowerment (ACE), a social justice-oriented nonprofit that works with immigrants that is behind the heat map.
  • "Just the simple threat of ICE presence is enough to keep somebody from voting," Rodriguez said. "It's all a coordinated effort to keep people away from voting and to make voting more confusing and less accessible."
  • She added the threat could be particularly acute for people coming from mixed-status households, where someone they live with isn't voting but isn't a citizen.

Catch up quick: Arizona's Republican-led state Senate considered a bill that would have required ICE agents at the polls this November, but it didn't pass. State Sen. Jake Hoffman (R) argued such a requirement would make elections safer, echoing the Trump administration.

  • "When voters see the rules applied fairly and consistently, confidence in the outcome follows," Hoffman said in a press release about the bill.
  • U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during his confirmation hearing that he didn't understand the concern about ICE agents being present at polls because "'if you're not a citizen you shouldn't be voting anyways, so technically there shouldn't be illegals at the polling spot."
  • Even though the Arizona bill failed, it put immigration advocates on high alert.

Zoom out: Laws governing how close any law enforcement officers — including local police — can be to polling places were imposed to avoid the potential that some voters may feel intimidate or think their right to vote is being suppressed.

  • Organizers behind Arizona's heat map app argue that it's not just undocumented immigrants who are at risk of being arrested if federal agents are at or nearby the polls. There have been several instances of Homeland Security's "roving patrols" arresting U.S. citizens and people outside the scope of targeted operations.
  • Critics of these operations argue that these erroneous encounters often stem from racial profiling that could impact any person of color or someone speaking a foreign language.
  • "They've arrested American citizens. They've gone after protesters on the streets. There was a fear factor when they were deployed, an intimidating factor as well, and so them being out in the community terrorizing folks will definitely have an impact on voter turnout," said Cesar Fierro, of Living United for Change in Arizona (LUCHA), an affiliated group with ACE.

The other side: "ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action," a DHS official said in an emailed statement.

  • The Arizona Secretary of State's office said in a statement that "the best way to address this potential issue is to do what election officials always do — prepare and plan for contingencies through trainings and building relationships between our county election officials and local law enforcement."

Between the lines: Despite the continued pursuits from the Trump administration to find and prosecute voter fraud, the numbers of ineligible people voting remains minute. Instances of noncitizens voting illegally are especially rare.

  • The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, tracks instances of illegal non-citizen voting and has not identified any such cases in Arizona.

item.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico sues White House over blocked access
item.description:
CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the White House, arguing the president and the administration violated their rights by blocking their access over the weekend.

Why it matters: Many presidents have had a contentious relationship with certain outlets, but none have gone so far as to unilaterally block them.

Zoom in: The three outlets filed their complaint when the courts opened Monday morning.

  • In the complaint, the plaintiffs argue the White House violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoint; and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process.
  • They ask the court to declare the ban unconstitutional, and have asked for an injunction to block the ban's enforcement and restore their access to The White House.

What they're saying: "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the three news organizations said in a joint statement on Monday.

  • "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," they said. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

Zoom out: The lawsuit is a historic show of solidarity amongst the banned outlets, as they and other newsrooms continue to face unprecedented pressure from The Trump administration.

  • Figures within the administration have argued the president has the right to ban reporters from certain spaces, but legal experts argue precedent overwhelmingly backs the news outlets.
  • "Once a government official has opened up a space to journalists more broadly, then that official can't then say, 'But you can't come in because I don't like your reporting … because of your viewpoint,'" Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, told Axios.

What to watch: The White House on Sunday released its weekly press pool rotation and CNN — which was the network responsible for carrying the video feed for the pool Monday — was not listed.

  • That means there will be no video coverage of the president today, and perhaps longer, depending on whether the court grants the plaintiffs in the case an injunction.
  • The other four broadcasters that split the video pool duty with CNN — ABC, CBS, NBC and FOX — have not yet released a statement about the situation.

This is a breaking news story.

item.title: Trump inaudible during White House TV pool blackout
item.description:
President Trump was inaudible during a press conference Monday after the TV pool suspended coverage, with White House-provided video carrying no usable audio of his remarks.

Why it matters: It's a remarkable and immediate ramification of Trump's attempt to limit pool access.

  • The pool serves hundreds of journalists, so losing independent TV coverage can limit what the media — and the public — can see and hear.

Driving the news: President Trump announced a ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Friday, confiscating their credentials on Saturday over what he termed "FAKE NEWS".

  • CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit on Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing the ban violates the First Amendment.
  • The decision to pull pooled TV coverage is a rare display of unified pushback from fiercely competitive networks against the administration's attempt to dictate what the public sees and how.

Thought bubble, via Axios' Brittany Gibson, one of the poolers: The White House Press Pool, by design and by necessity, is a collaborative effort amongst the nation's top news outlets.

  • These outlets, Axios included, are daily witnesses to arguably the most powerful office in the world and its revolving occupants. The daily reports of what we're able to see, hear, photograph are carefully and quickly shared for the public record and are part of holding the office accountable to the people.

What the pool is

How it works: The White House press pool is a rotating group of journalists who stay by the president's side throughout his public appearances and share their reporting, audio and footage with the rest of the media.

  • The pool includes about 20 journalists. They travel with Trump on Air Force One and cram into the Oval Office, providing updates.
  • The TV coverage relies on five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC — that take turns providing live footage.

What the pool does

The big picture: Trump is constantly on the move, so the pool makes it easier and less expensive to document his whereabouts.

  • The pool documents details like when The Beast — Trump's armored car — arrives at a location.
  • It also ensures coverage if the president needs to address the nation at a moment's notice

What they're saying: "So this isn't just DC insider access journalism," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, tells Axios.

  • "If you're living in Wyoming or Arizona or Chicago, it's very likely that the White House news you're reading originates from the press pool."

Zoom in: "The president is a walking news story," Stern says.

  • "[T]he press pool has been devalued by the president's conduct. The press pool is not getting honest and thoughtful insights from this president."
  • "That being said, that's still newsworthy. The way this president behaves is a news story. The fact that the president, in the midst of war, is rambling on about vanity projects is newsworthy. The fact that the president keeps berating female reporters is newsworthy."

What the TV blackout means

Without a TV pool crew, there is little independent broadcast video of the president's restricted-access events.

  • C-SPAN said it would not show Trump's White House helipad ribbon-cutting "because it relies on the TV pool and had no feed.
  • The blackout has limits: The White House pool won't provide a camera for Trump's UN trip, but the UN is expected to broadcast General Assembly proceedings with its own cameras.

The bottom line: The TV pool gives the public an independent audiovisual record of presidential events that otherwise may be seen only through government-provided cameras.

Go deeper: CNN, MS NOW, Politico sues White House over blocked access

item.title: "National security" becomes Trump's executive sledgehammer
item.description:
What do a White House ban on journalists, a 250-foot arch near the nation's capital and Greenland have in common?

  • President Trump needs all of them for national security purposes, he and his administration have argued.

Why it matters: As he's unilaterally shattered presidential norms, Trump has justified his sweeping policy priorities with a familiar two-word rationale: national security.

Driving the news: On the morning that the three banned outlets (CNN, MS NOW and Politico) sued the administration, Trump claimed that "FAKE NEWS" is "a threat to our National Security."

  • It's not the first time the administration has said its press restrictions were a national security must: That was also part of the reasoning for new rules for Pentagon reporters, a war on leakers and subpoenas of journalists.

National security purposes are a broad bucket that the president has also used to justify his D.C. redesign:

  • Trump pitched his proposed "triumphal arch" as a dual-use facility housing snipers, drones and ammunition storage "for National Security purposes." That's also why the president was adamant his White House ballroom project must proceed (after he demolished the East Wing).
  • The White House declined to comment beyond the president's post.

Zoom out: The national security rationale has also fueled the administration's deregulatory AI approach.

  • Earlier this month, Justice Department attorneys argued that laws that get in the way of a growing AI industry "threaten national security" in a statement of interest backing AI companies in The New York Times' copyright infringement lawsuit.

What they're saying: The executive's use of national security as a justification for policy can trigger "extreme deference" in the courts, says Kimberly Wehle, a University of Baltimore law professor.

  • Wehle notes the expanded executive power seen in Trump 2.0 has its origins in the Bush-era advancement of the unitary executive theory — though the national psyche today does not necessarily reflect the urgency of the 9/11 era.
  • "It appears that the Trump administration has taken a page from that era and understands that it's easier to justify power from the standpoint of the public, and even in the courts, if you can say it's in the interest of national security," she says.

Friction point: The argument hasn't always found a receptive audience.

  • An appeals court considering Trump's White House ballroom project concluded last month that "[w]hile this court accords great weight and deference to invocations of national security and the safety of the President, such arguments are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card."
  • Elizabeth Goitein, senior director of the Brennan Center's Liberty and National Security Program, says the ambiguity of "national security" has moved "toward this dangerous zone where the words … become a blank check" and "take on this talismanic significance in the courts."
  • Trump didn't start it, she says. But "Trump's willingness to claim national security for things that so patently have nothing to do with national security is at a new level."

Worth noting: The administration has also busted norms in the more traditional national security realm.

  • After months of demanding U.S. ownership of Greenland as a national security necessity, Trump announced last week that the U.S. struck a deal with Denmark and Greenland to give America "permanent control over security" on the island, where the U.S. already had military access.
  • South of the border, the administration has waged a year-long campaign against alleged narcoterrorists, killing some 230 people in boat strikes and fueling broad international law concerns.
  • And while immigration policy is a key pillar of the nation's security apparatus, Trump's far-reaching crackdown has lumped international students, Temporary Protected Status holders and travelers from certain designated nations together under the guise of national security threats.

The bottom line: National security concerns have long been fuel for the expansion of presidential authority.

  • Trump, however, has used national security to justify acting not only as the commander in chief, but, recently, as a builder in chief and editor in chief as well.

Go deeper: Trump's proposed Washington arch to become sniper, drone facility

item.title: Ahead of Sam Altman's UN address, OpenAI proposes new ways to track AI misalignment risks
item.description:
OpenAI on Monday released international AI safety standards as world leaders, namely the U.S. and China, weigh how to mitigate risk.

Why it matters: The U.S. approach to coordinating on AI risk with China will be heavily informed by industry recommendations.

Driving the news: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend discussed a U.S.-China AI dialogue to notify the other country when AI incidents reached national security risk levels.

  • The devil is in the details and OpenAI is proposing solutions that CEO Sam Altman will cover in his address at the United Nations Security Council in New York on Wednesday.

What they're saying: OpenAI recommends leveraging AI safety institutes around the world to facilitate standard-setting through the U.S. Center for AI Security and Innovation, which is part of the Commerce Department.

  • The company also recommends shared global measurements for classifying incidents and how to track, report and respond to alignment issues.
  • The goal is to have international standards for incidents that happen before deployment in test settings and those that occur in the real world, an OpenAI official told Axios.

What we're watching: Expect AI labs to continue chiming in as all eyes are on President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's meetings and a state dinner featuring industry heavy hitters later this week.

item.title: Exclusive: How Sen. Schatz is talking about climate in an affordability crisis
item.description:
Americans are "connecting the dots" between climate and affordability strain, Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) said Monday at an Axios House event on the sidelines of Climate Week and the UN General Assembly.

Why it matters: But as pocketbook issues dominate a critical midterm race, Schatz says that doesn't mean the first thing he mentions to constituents is climate. Still, climate-tangent conversations — like utility prices and the data center boom — are looming over the polls.

Driving the news: "I think we should talk about climate in the context of people not being able to afford their lives," Schatz told Axios' Ben Geman, pointing to insurance non-renewals, soaring gas prices and rising utility bills.

  • "It's not that difficult anymore for us to be able to say, look, one of the reasons things are getting more expensive is we're not addressing the climate crisis," he said, criticizing the federal government's renewables roadblocks.
  • "The climate imperatives used to have to be balanced against people's pocketbooks, and now they are perfectly lined up," he added. "We do not have to make trade-offs. They are deciding to make the planet worse and make your pocketbook situation worse."

Catch up quick: Schatz has been a leading congressional voice on climate issues, representing a heavily petroleum-dependent U.S. state with high energy prices that's at particular risk from the impacts of climate change.

  • The state has taken on an ambitious clean energy initiative that aims for 100% renewable energy by 2035 on the neighbor islands, including Maui and Hawaiʻi.

Friction point: The sweeping GOP budget bill signed into law by President Trump last year phased out wind, solar, and electric vehicle subsidies that the prior administration championed as tools to bolster clean tech.

  • It's one front in Trump's broader rollback of Biden-era climate policies, including moves to kill regulations and a slowdown in permitting of renewables projects.
  • In particular, administration officials have targeted wind power, which Trump has repeatedly criticized. Still, the AI boom is expected to drive a surge in clean energy this year.

Go deeper: New signs Iran war is boosting clean energy

item.title: Far-right AfD wins again as Germany's Merz slides
item.description:
Germany's ruling center-right party, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union, was shut out of a state parliament for the first time Sunday as the far-right Alternative for Germany scored its second victory this month.

Why it matters: The result marks the third state election AfD has won — and its second this month — underscoring its growing strength even as Germany's other major parties refuse to govern with it.

Driving the news: Merz, who has low approval ratings, told reporters that "reforms have to come."

  • AfD won about 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the CDU recorded its worst result in any German state election since World War II. The CDU fell from 13% to 4.9% and lost all representation.
  • In Berlin's state election, the Left more than doubled its vote share to 25.7% and finished first for the first time.

Flashback: AfD won its first state election in Thuringia in 2024, though other parties kept it out of government because they refused to enter into a coalition.

  • Earlier this month, it won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt, but fell just three seats short of a majority. It is now seeking enough outside support to form Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.
  • Vice President JD Vance met with AfD's co-leader days before last year's federal election and told the Munich Security Conference there was "no room for firewalls," referring to mainstream parties' refusal to govern with the AfD.

The big picture: Germany's political firewall against AfD is rooted partly in the country's post-World War II consensus against returning the far-right to government and has been reinforced by intelligence concerns about extremism within the party.

  • Germany's domestic intelligence service continues to monitor AfD nationally as a suspected extremist organization. A court in February blocked the agency from classifying the entire party as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization while a broader case proceeds.
  • The anti-migration party calls for "remigration" — large-scale deportations and encouraging immigrants to leave. It also wants to abandon the euro, lift Russian sanctions and end weapons deliveries to Ukraine.

What they're saying: AfD leader Alice Weidel called on Merz to "face the consequences" of the CDU's losses and said her party had displaced the CDU as Germany's "people's party."

  • She wrote on X the CDU "will have to think very carefully about whether it can continue with this firewall policy, especially in eastern Germany" and called for the parties to sit down for talks.

The bottom line: AfD's rise is reshaping politics in Europe's largest economy, putting growing pressure on Germany's governing center and the firewall that has kept the party out of power.

item.title: Trump weighed strikes against Houthis in Yemen before holding off
item.description:
President Trump over the weekend considered ordering a strike against the Houthis in Yemen before deciding to hold off for now, two U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: Trump was caught between wanting to help his friend and ally, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and avoiding getting entangled on a new front in the Middle East.

Catch up quick: Ten days ago, bin Salman (MBS) called Trump twice on the same day, urging him to launch strikes against the Houthis as the Iran-backed group closed in on a vital Red Sea chokepoint.

  • Trump rejected the request and agreed only to help the Saudis with intelligence and targeting data.
  • U.S. officials said at the time they wouldn't take military action as long as the Houthis did not interrupt non-Saudi ship traffic in the Red Sea.
  • Several days later, U.S. diplomats met with Houthi officials and received assurances that the rebel group has no intention of closing the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Behind the scenes: But late last week the Saudis, who were having trouble pushing back on Houthi advances, again asked Trump to take military action in Yemen, the two U.S. officials said.

  • They said that over the weekend Trump held consultations with his senior advisers about the possibility of strikes against the Houthis.
  • One U.S. official said the commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), Adm. Brad Cooper, prepared options for airstrikes in Yemen and presented them to Secretary of Defense Hegseth on Saturday.
  • But Trump ultimately decided to hold off, another U.S. official said.
  • The New York Times first reported about Trump's deliberations around the possible strike in Yemen.
  • The White House and the Saudi embassy in Washington declined to comment.

What they're saying: "The president changed his mind and did not want to open a Pandora's box by striking because it could cause the Houthis to hold the Bab al-Mandeb at risk and create a second choke point," Alex Plitsas, a fellow at the Atlantic Council and former Pentagon official, told Axios.

  • That "would cause oil prices to spike further when the Saudis were supposed to take the lead on dealing with the Houthi problem," he added.

State of play: The Saudis, together with Yemeni government forces, have been working for two weeks on a counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, but it has been delayed several times, sources say.

  • In the meantime, the Houthis have been escalating strikes against Saudi Arabia. Over the weekend, they launched a missile toward Riyadh.

item.title: Exclusive: Beshear says next president must go big on housing
item.description:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear signaled in an interview with Axios that he would put America's housing affordability crisis at the center of his campaign if he ran for president in 2028.

Why it matters: It's the latest sign that Beshear, who just kicked off a national book tour, is moving closer to a bid for the White House.

Driving the news: Beshear said the next president should pursue a massive housing initiative — with strict guidelines to ensure the money is spent quickly.

  • "There's a chance for the next presidential administration or the next Congress to make a big, bold investment in housing that could have us building millions of units all over the United States," he said.
  • "We cannot do this in drips and drabs. It can't be mild investments over a period of time."

Echoing the "Abundance" movement, which calls for slashing regulations in order to lower housing costs, Beshear said federal dollars sent to states should be used quickly or withdrawn.

  • "If you tie the federal dollars to that timing, you will break through the regulation and the NIMBYism," he said.
  • Beshear declined to put a specific price tag on his vision, saying that those details could be discussed with lawmakers. But he said $150 billion in federal spending could theoretically lead to $1 trillion of housing being built if enough outside financing were leveraged.

By the numbers: Escalating home prices have become a major political issue in recent years. Sixty-four percent of American adults say they're "very concerned" about the cost of housing, according to a Pew Research Center poll in July.

The intrigue: After talking policy, we asked Beshear about rumors swirling in Democratic circles that he could announce a run for president as soon as December.

  • "I would tell you that that is solely a rumor," he said of the winter timeline. "I haven't made any final decisions yet."
  • But, sounding as if he's close to making up his mind, Beshear added, "Listen, I don't want to leave a broken country to my kids."

item.title: Many ex-aides to Harris betting against a 2028 run
item.description:
Many of those who know Kamala Harris best think she ultimately won't run for the White House in 2028.

Why it matters: What the former vice president decides to do is one of the biggest X factors in the next presidential contest: Early polls suggest Harris is the frontrunner to be the Democratic nominee, and if she opted out, it would scramble the primary.

Zoom in: Over the past year, a surprisingly large number of former aides, surrogates and donors to Harris have told Axios they believe she won't launch another campaign.

  • They argue that the moves she's making — hitting the trail for midterm candidates, going on the podcast circuit, and writing a book — might make her look like a contender-in-waiting, but actually amount to her simply trying to maintain influence.
  • Harris has said publicly and privately she hasn't made up her mind yet, and some of her former aides concede they could be wrong — or could even be "wishcasting" because they don't want her to pursue another bid.

This week, we surveyed eight former Harris aides and advisers, including those who worked for her at a senior level, to get their most up-to-date read. Only one thought Harris probably will run. Two said it's a coin-flip, and five said she likely won't. Here's why:

  1. She's doing "the bare minimum" to stay in the 2028 conversation, as one past aide put it. Harris' former staffers argue that if she were gung-ho about running she'd be hiring more, traveling more, and inserting herself into policy debates more often.
  2. She's a rational actor. Former aides say Harris is well aware of the hurdles that would await her if she ran again. "She's a realist and an astute political observer, and she knows her candidacy could get bogged down in a 2024 rearview mirror," said a second former aide.
  3. The money might not be there. Many high-dollar donors are still furious about Harris' loss and don't want her to run again. Top Democratic donor Reid Hoffman said last week that she'd face "a very challenging path" in 2028. Some of her former financial backers are signaling support for other potential candidates, such as Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
  4. She isn't an egomaniac. Sure, this is self-serving. But multiple people who worked for Harris say she lacks the "sociopathic" belief — their words, not ours — that it's she and she alone who should be president.
  5. Some tea leaves suggest she's lukewarm on running. Harris effectively gave up control of her @KamalaHQ social media account, and bought an $8 million house in Malibu with her husband. Also, her top aide Kirsten Allen left her team recently, though Harris still speaks with her.

What they're saying: A former Harris aide connected to Axios by her current team put the odds of another run at "50-50," saying the former VP "is a very methodical decision-maker" who will weigh "the moment that we're in."

  • This former aide pushed back on the notion that money could be a problem, pointing to Harris' massive email fundraising list and arguing that high-dollar donors won't determine the next nominee. They also said her team doesn't need to be bigger when the focus is on the midterms.
  • "There will be a lot of people who will feel a lot of urgency to announce as soon as possible," the former aide said. "I think the vice president doesn't necessarily have to be on that timeline."

The lone former Harris staffer who told us they expect her to run gave it a "55% chance," noting that Harris has been ramping up her calls to Democratic officials and activists.

  • "I think there's a lot of wishcasting that maybe Kamala will come to her senses and not do it," this person said.
  • Harris definitely is keeping the door open to another bid, including by gearing up to campaign this fall for battleground candidates such as Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Nevada gubernatorial hopeful Aaron Ford.
  • But many former aides who think Harris would be a good president say they don't want her to run again because they seriously doubt she could win, given her record. One way to view their arguments: They're trying to persuade her to stay out of the race.

David Plouffe, Harris' 2024 senior adviser, was blunt about the headwinds she would face in a third national campaign, even as he acknowledged she'd begin in an enviable position.

  • "Her strongest day will be her first day in the campaign," Plouffe told "Pod Save America," predicting Harris' support likely would erode as the race developed.

The bottom line: People who talk to Harris say she's genuinely undecided about 2028, but political insiders will keep scrutinizing her every move for signs of what she'll do next.

  • During a recent podcast interview, she told former soccer star Megan Rapinoe: "I don't know how to live and not serve."

Axios' Alex Thompson contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump to meet with Zelensky as Russia-Ukraine attacks intensify
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after a phone call with President Trump on Sunday that the two will meet this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Why it matters: The meeting comes as the White House works to broker an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to take reciprocal steps to deescalate and resume negotiations — and as fighting between the two sides has intensified in recent days.

  • Zelensky's chief negotiator and the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, Rustem Umerov, told Axios he's been working with White House envoys in recent days to organize the meeting, which is expected to happen Tuesday.

Driving the news: The meeting will take place several days after Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill and approved the biggest arms deal between the U.S. and Ukraine since assuming office — two steps Ukraine has been pushing for months.

What he's saying: "An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelensky wrote on X.

  • Zelensky said Ukraine is ready "to take really serious steps" to reach a deescalation deal with Russia.

Behind the scenes: A source familiar with the call said Trump repeatedly asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The strikes are driving up global diesel prices.

  • "The word diesel came up many times during the call," the source said.

The intrigue: Earlier this week the Kyiv Independent reported that the Ukrainian government was "growing increasingly frustrated" with White House envoy Steve Witkoff.

  • The story came out several days after Witkoff and Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time since the war began.
  • Umerov told Axios the story was false.
  • "I believe that the work of American negotiators should be assessed by people who are directly involved in the negotiation process and work closely with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," he said.
  • He added that he's been working with Witkoff and Kushner on a daily basis over the last year. "Our main focus is on finding solutions for ending the war and gaining security guarantees and prosperity to Ukrainian people," he added.
  • Umerov said the negotiations are under close public and media scrutiny and therefore "it comes with criticism."
  • "Nevertheless, we need to stay focused. Steve has done a great job with us. We do not waste time and stay focused on finding solutions," he said.

State of play: Umerov said significant progress has been made in the talks. "In particular, the number of stumbling blocks reduced from dozens to essentially one or two key issues that remain subject to negotiations," he said.

  • "The trend is positive. The U.S. is super focused on the issue of stopping the war in Ukraine. The U.S. understands the situation on the battlefield, and signals to everyone that this terrible war should end," Umerov said.

Yes, but: Hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have escalated in recent days, with both sides conducting more long-range attacks.

  • On Sunday, Ukraine launched a missile attack on Moscow and hit an oil refinery. Russia has been launching missiles at Kyiv and other major cities almost every day in recent weeks.
  • While Russia has signaled willingness to consider steps to deescalate ahead of winter — and a resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine — there has been little progress towards an actual deal.
